verdicts.reason: Guessable by elimination: the three distractors are all physiological absurdities ('talking makes your muscles work less hard', 'walking together uses a different set of muscles', 'two people always walk faster than one' — note the giveaway 'always'), so the correct option is the only one that is even about how effort feels. Replace at least two distractors with plausible psychological mechanisms (e.g. 'you stop keeping track of how far you have gone', 'you set off before you can talk yourself out of it') so the reader has to know which one is right.

Distractor quality. 'Everyone gets the same amount of benefit from it' is plainly false, 'It only works if everyone does the same activity' is defeated by its own 'only', and 'The youngest person sets the pace' is unrelated to the question asked. The correct option is also the only figuratively phrased one, which makes it stand out visually. Also overlaps heavily with SF-TRV-000320, which teaches the same time-anchoring point in the same slice — keep one.

Textbook answer-shape giveaway: the options are 'Only A', 'Only B', 'Both', 'Neither', and 'Both' is the correct one. In an app whose whole voice is that everyone's effort counts, a nine-year-old will pick it without knowing anything about relative effort. The teaching point is good — keep it, but rewrite the options so the inclusive answer is not the only kind one (e.g. make a distractor 'Both, but only once they are out of breath', which is also inclusive and still wrong).

Two defensible answers. Option 1, 'Other people remind you more often than you remember', is a real and well-documented mechanism for why shared habits stick, so marking it wrong makes the item feel arbitrary. Either make that distractor clearly inadequate or rewrite the stem to ask specifically why it holds up even when nobody reminds you. Separately, the explanation ('skipping it is a small thing you would be doing to them too') leans on obligation to others in a way that sits awkwardly against the app's no-shame rule — consider framing it as shared rather than owed.

A judgement call presented as having one right answer. 'Say nothing about the gap and get straight on with it' and 'Remind them how well they were doing before' are both things thoughtful people genuinely do, and the explanation asserts the chosen option 'beats both silence and a post-mortem' without any basis offered. `editorial` confidence is fine for an opinion, but a trivia item marks three defensible choices as errors. Either reframe as a Rickie aside rather than a quiz, or make the distractors things that are actually unhelpful (e.g. 'Ask them to promise it will not happen again').

True (inter-individual variability in training response is well documented), safe, non-comparative, and all four options are beliefs people actually hold. The explanation adds information rather than restating the option.

Firmness: 'Watching somebody do a thing ordinarily is the most reliable teaching there is' is a superlative the evidence does not support — parental modelling is associated with children's activity, it is not established as the single most reliable form of teaching. Soften to something like 'is a large part of how children learn'. Also two of the distractors ('It guarantees the child is doing it correctly', 'Children need supervision for most kinds of movement') do not answer the question asked, which narrows the field to two before the reader thinks.

States one side of a genuinely mixed picture as fact. A visibly stronger partner can also raise effort and motivation (the Köhler effect is well replicated), so 'It motivates the other person to catch up' is not simply wrong, and 'The stronger person gets a poorer workout from it' is often true as well. The stem says 'tends to happen', which claims a direction the literature does not settle. Mark `contested` and say so in the text, or narrow the stem to the specific case the explanation is really about (a mismatch neither person can ignore).

Only one option is on topic. The question asks about consistency; three of the four options are about distance or effort, so the reader can select the right answer purely by matching subject matter without knowing anything about dogs or commitment. Rewrite the distractors as competing explanations for consistency (e.g. 'the dog is pleased to see you go', 'the walk happens at the same time each day').

Two throwaway distractors — 'Making sure nobody notices that they stopped' and 'Choosing an activity that person was never keen on' are not things anyone would propose — leaving one real alternative. It is also a near-duplicate of SF-TRV-000312: both items' correct answer is 'anchor the routine to a time, not a person'. Cut one of the two or give this one a distinct angle.

Overstated for a `simplified` item with no source. Choice and autonomy do improve adherence, but 'far more likely to turn up' and 'The activity matters much less than whose idea it was' are much firmer than the evidence, which shows a modest effect. Soften to 'more likely', drop the second sentence's comparative claim, or cite a self-determination-theory source and promote to `established`.

Well hedged ('can turn', 'sometimes useful and sometimes'), teaches a real and non-obvious idea, and the explanation gives both sides rather than restating the option. Distractor 'Targets work better for groups than for individuals' is genuinely tempting.
Safe and on-rubric — it explicitly rejects 'push through it anyway' and treats the tiredness as real rather than as something to argue with. Age-appropriate and genuinely useful.
Soft, hedged ('often'), harmless, and teaches a real framing effect. 'Without noticing' in the stem does enough work to separate it from the 'more energy when rested' distractor.

The stem telegraphs the answer. 'if nothing is done about it' signals that the right option is the one mentioning what happens when something IS done, and only option 2 does — it is also the longest. The underlying claim is sound, so this is purely an options fix: drop the qualifier from the stem, or move 'practicing it slows that down' into the explanation and make the options compete on what actually happens to balance.

THE CITATION IS WRONG. This is the only `established` item in the slice and its sole source, PMID 2360822, is 'Pentoxifylline modulates meningeal inflammation in experimental bacterial meningitis' (Antimicrob Agents Chemother, 1990) — nothing to do with strength training. The paper the explanation is describing is Fiatarone et al., 'High-intensity strength training in nonagenarians', JAMA 1990, which is PMID 2342214. The claim is true and the item is otherwise good; swap the source to https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2342214/ and re-check every other `established` citation in this batch, because the validator only checks that `sources` is non-empty, not that the URL resolves to the right paper.

Stated far more firmly than the evidence supports. 'Adolescent awkwardness' is poorly supported and actively disputed: a systematic review of sensorimotor function in adolescence found inconsistent results, several longitudinal studies aligned on peak height velocity found no decline (strength, speed and flexibility rose through the growth spurt), and a 2025 narrative review concludes there is no consensus definition and limited empirical evidence for the phenomenon at all. The 'brain holds an out-of-date map of your limb length' mechanism is a popular explanation, not an established one. Either mark `contested` and say in the text that it is argued over, or cut the item. Do not ship it as `simplified` fact to teenagers who will read it as a description of themselves.

True and well supported, and the explanation earns its place by naming what independence concretely means (getting out of a chair, carrying shopping) rather than restating the option. Minor: 'It keeps everyday independence' reads slightly clipped.

Formatting tell — the correct option is the only one beginning 'No —' and the only one containing a dash, so it is visually distinct before it is read. Combined with 'Children only benefit from organized sport', which its own 'only' defeats, the field collapses to two. Rephrase the correct option to match the others' shape and make the sport distractor plausible (e.g. 'Organised sport covers it more completely than play does').

The correct option is conspicuously the only hedged, two-clause, nuanced one, which is the standard tell — readers learn to pick the careful-sounding answer. 'It is fixed from birth and never changes' is also a throwaway nobody would choose. Additionally, 'less so in active people' is largely cross-sectional evidence and is stated here as settled causation; soften to something like 'and people who keep doing quick-response things tend to slow less', or source it.

The question's premise is not established and recent evidence points the other way. A 2025 systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression found advancing age is NOT associated with greater exercise-induced muscle damage, and that older adults reported substantially less soreness at 48 and 72 hours than younger ones; a 2023 scoping review on recovery from resistance exercise in older adults concluded the findings are too inconsistent to support clear recommendations. This item asserts 'recovery tends to take longer as you get older' in the stem as settled fact and then gives training advice built on it. Rewrite the stem so it does not presuppose the effect, mark `contested`, and say in the text that it is argued over — or cut the item. Two of the distractors ('Muscles become permanently more fragile', 'The body stops repairing muscle after middle age') are throwaways regardless.

The claim is true, but the item is unguessable-proof in the wrong direction: 'There is no age at which starting stops helping' is the answer this app always gives, and 'It depends entirely on your family history' is defeated by its own 'entirely'. It is also redundant with SF-TRV-000326 in the same slice, which already makes the never-too-late point with better distractors and an actual study behind it. Cut this one or give it a specific, checkable payload (what late starters actually gain, and how fast).

Mechanism question that genuinely requires knowing the answer, and 'Pressure forces minerals into the bone from the blood' is a properly tempting distractor. Claim (bone remodels in response to mechanical load) is solidly established and the explanation explains rather than restates.

The correct option is the grammatical odd one out: three options open 'A rule... / The idea... / A gradual loss...' and the fourth opens 'Tissue kept...', so it can be picked on shape alone. 'The idea that rest is always harmful' is also a throwaway. Separately, 'Tissue kept in proportion to its demand' is abstract phrasing for a stated min_age of 9 — the explanation is clearer than the option it explains, which suggests the option should be rewritten in the explanation's language.

Claim is fine but the item is guessable without knowing anything: all three distractors are absolutes ('always indicates', 'the only remedy', 'only affects people who exercise') and the key is the only hedged option, so a test-wise nine-year-old picks it by pattern. Rewrite at least two distractors as plausible non-absolute beliefs (e.g. 'Yes, and it usually means you slept badly'). Also consider naming the actual red line in the explanation — stiffness lasting more than about an hour most mornings is the thing worth asking about — rather than the vague 'severe or persistent'.

The keyed answer is wrong on the substance and the explanation understates a real danger to the exact audience. Falls are the leading cause of injury death in adults 65+; about half of fatal falls involve traumatic brain injury, and falls cause the large majority of hip fractures, which frequently end independent living. 'The fall itself is often survivable' is a minimising framing of that. Worse, distractor C ('Falls are much more common than in younger people') is simply true — roughly 1 in 4 adults 65+ falls each year — so the item has two defensible answers and keys the weaker one. If the post-fall fear cycle is the lesson worth teaching, ask about it directly ('After a fall, what often does damage even when nothing is broken?') and keep the physical injury risk in the explanation instead of waving it away.
True at the level given, mechanism actually explained, distractors all plausible beliefs.

Two problems. (1) Options A ('how athletic they were as a teenager') and C ('whether they played sport at school') say essentially the same thing, so a reader eliminates both on the logic that they cannot both be wrong separately — that plus the weak 'height and build' leaves one option standing. Collapse them into one and add a genuinely competing predictor. (2) 'The best predictor' is a superlative empirical claim carried by a `simplified` label with no sources; recent activity is strongly associated with late-life function but calling it the best predictor outruns what is cited. Either soften to 'which of these matters most' or attach a source.
Correct, safe, and the explanation teaches the discriminating cue (sharp vs dull) rather than restating the option.

The rule as stated in the option — 'effort builds gradually; a warning is sudden' — misses and actively miscategorises overuse injury, which is the most common way a beginner gets hurt and which builds gradually by definition. A reader applying this rule would file a slowly worsening tendon or shin pain under 'ordinary effort'. The explanation's 'not a perfect rule' hedge does not cover that specific failure; name it (pain that grows session on session, or that is still there the next day, is also a warning). Option D ('there is no reliable way to tell them apart') is a bare dismissal distractor and should be replaced.
Accurate on the Valsalva effect, appropriately unalarming, and the explanation gives an actionable fix (breathe out on the effort). Distractors are all things people actually believe.

Guessable by shape: the key is the longest option and the only one with two clauses, and it is the only one that mentions a doctor. Separately, distractor B is not wrong enough to be a distractor — lying down is legitimate first aid for dizziness, so a reader who knows that is penalised for knowing it. Make B clearly worse (e.g. 'lie flat and then finish the session'), and even out option lengths.
Notably well-handled firmness: 'it reduces risk; it does not abolish it' is exactly the right register, and B is a useful wrong belief to knock down rather than a throwaway.

Right advice, wrong reason, and the wrong line drawn. Standard guidance splits on fever and systemic symptoms (fever, body aches, deep fatigue) rather than on 'anything chest-related' — that is the above-the-neck rule, and the reason behind it is cardiac strain and impaired heat regulation while febrile, with a small myocarditis risk, not 'mostly buys you a longer illness'. That last claim is stated as fact and is not well supported. Rewrite the explanation around fever as the stop signal, and keep the chest-symptom caution as an addition rather than the whole caveat.
Concrete, useful, and the explanation earns its place with real examples rather than restating the option.
Matches current drink-to-thirst guidance for ordinary activity and correctly declines to treat more as safer. No meal/body framing issues.
Honestly labelled `editorial`, so no sourcing obligation, and it points toward a professional rather than giving a diagnosis.

The advice is good but the explanation invents a statistic: 'most restart injuries come from resuming at the old level' is an unsourced quantified claim under a `simplified` label. This is the firmness failure the rubric calls out. Say it as the pattern it is ('a common way people get hurt on a restart is picking up where they left off') or attach a source. The option text itself is fine.
Real mechanism, correctly explained, and it beats the folk answers without mocking them.
Talk test is a well-established crude intensity gauge and the explanation says so without overselling it.
Correct on painless crepitus, and it carries the pain/swelling caveat without turning it into a scare.
Explains the mechanism (momentum masking the pattern) rather than restating the option.

'Often within the first few minutes' is firmer than the evidence. The acute-exercise literature generally finds mood benefit from bouts of about ten minutes upward, measured during and after the bout, and affect during effort depends on intensity — above the ventilatory threshold it typically gets worse before it gets better. A child who feels nothing at minute two and concludes it is not working is the failure mode. Rephrase to something like 'often within a single short session, not weeks' and add a source, or downgrade the timing claim.

No single defensible right answer. Distractor B ('it gives you time to think without interruption') is at least as good an explanation as the key, and C is not far behind, so a reader who thinks about it carefully can land on B and be marked wrong. The key also asserts a cognitive mechanism ('loosening attention lets connections surface') that is a hypothesis, not a settled finding, under a `simplified` label with no sources — the walking/creativity effect is reasonably well evidenced but its mechanism is not. Either narrow the question so only one option fits, or relabel and source it.
Honestly labelled `editorial`; distractors are all real beliefs people hold.
Editorial and labelled as such; the explanation gives a concrete image (the two-minute version on a terrible day) rather than restating the option.
Consistent with distraction-versus-rumination findings, stated moderately, no diagnosis or medical advice, age-appropriate.
Kind, non-shaming, editorial and labelled as such.

The stem asks for an effect, but the keyed option states a mechanism ('measures you against a starting point that is not yours'), which is the only option not in effect-form and the only critical one among three positive ones - both tells. Worse, distractor index 2 ('helps most when the other person is close to your level') is broadly supported by social comparison research, so a knowledgeable reader is punished. Either rewrite the stem to ask what is wrong with comparison, or replace that distractor.

The explanation's first sentence is a verbatim restatement of the keyed option and never names or explains the mechanism (loss aversion / the value already banked). Also 'a well-documented quirk' is firmer than warranted: loss aversion's robustness and magnitude are actively disputed (Gal & Rucker 2018, 'The Loss of Loss Aversion'). Name the effect, say why losses weigh more, and soften to 'a well-known pattern' or label the item contested.

'Anchoring ... outperforms reminders' is a firm head-to-head comparative claim with confidence 'simplified' and no source. The peer-reviewed evidence does not support it that flatly - reminder and prompt interventions perform well in large behaviour-change trials, and the anchoring-beats-reminders figures in circulation come from popular blogs, not trials. Drop the comparison and just explain why an existing routine is a reliable cue, or cite a real trial.
True, well-pitched, anti-shame, and the explanation adds the real idea (the pattern, not the day).
Editorial framing is honestly labelled and the reference-point point is genuinely useful.
Deliberately modest claim, correctly labelled editorial, no medical overreach. One of the better items.
Poor sleep raising perceived exertion at a fixed workload is solid, and the explanation adds the distinction between the work and the reading of it.
Neural adaptation dominating early balance gains is well supported, and 'almost entirely' is defensible for days-scale balance practice.

Safety: the rubric bars eyes-closed movement, and this item invites a child or a senior to test it by closing their eyes while balancing with no caveat at all. Add an explicit instruction that eyes-closed balance is only done seated or with a hand on something solid. Separately, the keyed option is the only one carrying its own mini-explanation ('; one input of three is gone'), which makes it pickable on form alone - move that clause into the explanation.
Good safety content, and the explanation gives the real reason (working at the edge of ability) rather than restating.

The citation is wrong. NBK556154 is 'Environmental Justice Concerns and the Proposed Atlantic Coast Pipeline Route in North Carolina' (RTI Press, 2018) - it has nothing to do with proprioception or physiology. This is the only item in the slice marked confidence 'established', and its single source does not support the claim. The claim itself is correct and the options are well built, so replace the source with a real one (e.g. StatPearls 'Physiology, Sensory System', NBK547656) and re-verify. Any other item in the library citing NBK556154 should be checked too.

Energy cost of walking on sand is 2.1-2.7x pavement and grass sits between, driven by work done deforming the substrate - the stated mechanism is right. Grass is the weaker half of the premise but not misleading.
Automatic postural responses do precede conscious awareness; explanation earns its place.

The keyed answer is near-tautological - 'turning is where control gets tested' is close to the definition of agility, so the item tests nothing. Option 0 ('straight-line movement does not build muscle') is a throwaway no reader would pick. Rework so the item teaches an actual mechanism (deceleration and re-acceleration load, changing the base of support under momentum) rather than restating the category.
Short frequent balance practice is consistent with standard fall-prevention programming, and the advice is safe.

Both the premise and the mechanism are stated far more firmly than the evidence supports, and the item is labelled 'simplified' rather than contested. The review literature on monopedal balance and limb dominance does not reach consensus, and several studies in sedentary adults, adolescents and athletes found no significant difference between legs - which means distractor index 2 ('balance is unrelated to which side you favor') is at least as defensible as the keyed answer. Either relabel as contested and say in the text that the evidence is mixed, or cut the item.
Attentional dissociation lowering perceived effort is sound, and the three distractors are all real misconceptions.
Circadian entrainment by morning light is solid, and distractor 2 ('sunlight is strongest then') is a good trap since it is false.
Practical, safe, and the explanation gives the reason rather than the rule.

Close, but this is a respiratory symptom in an app read by nine-year-olds, and the item leads with 'it is usually dryness', which normalises a sign that can be exercise-induced asthma. The escalation line, 'persistent tightness is worth asking about', never says who to ask. Make it concrete - tell an adult, and see a doctor if it keeps happening - and put the caveat before the reassurance rather than last.

Correctly hedged to association rather than cause, and the text does say what is argued over, which is what 'contested' requires. Minor construction tell: the keyed option is the only tentatively worded one among three firm claims, so a test-savvy reader can pick it on tone.

Editorial, honestly labelled, and the explanation does the work the answer option does not. Options 2 and 3 overlap enough that a test-wise reader can pair-eliminate them, but option 1 is a genuine competitor.

The question says 'headphones', the answer says 'the rhythm you hear' — a podcast or audiobook has no rhythm, so the stem does not support the answer. Say 'music with a steady beat' in the question. Also soften the firmness: spontaneous (uninstructed) entrainment is modest and mainly occurs when the track's tempo is already close to your natural cadence, not for any tempo you play.
Mechanism and the ten-minute figure are both well supported, and the framing avoids any diet or medical advice. Distractor 0 is a bit of a throwaway but the other two are fair.

'What is the MOST COMMON reason people skip an outdoor walk' is an empirical claim about population frequency, answered from editorial opinion with no data behind it — exactly the over-firm framing the rubric warns about. Either cite survey evidence, or rewrite the stem as a claim you can actually stand behind, e.g. 'What is a common trap when deciding whether to walk outdoors?'

Source is Lally et al. 2010 (EJSP, doi 10.1002/ejsp.674) and it says what the item says: median 66 days, range 18-254. '21 days' is a genuinely attractive distractor, so the item is not a freebie despite being the only hedged option. Minor: explanation says 'studies' plural for one cited study.
Honestly labelled editorial, all four options are things people actually believe, and the explanation adds a reason rather than restating.

Half of this is evidence-backed and half is folklore presented as fact. Lally 2010 found a single missed opportunity did not materially affect habit formation — that part is fine. But 'two in a row is where a habit starts becoming a thing you used to do' is the 'never miss twice' rule of thumb from Atomic Habits / Tiny Habits, not a measured threshold, and it is baked into the correct option itself ('unless a second one follows'). Either drop the two-day threshold from the option and explanation, or mark it plainly as a rule of thumb rather than a finding.

Self-monitoring reactivity is well replicated, and the item is careful to say 'shift' rather than claiming a direction. No body or weight framing. Distractor 0 is true-but-not-an-answer, which is a good distractor rather than a bad one.

Source resolves to Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006, Adv. Exp. Soc. Psychol. 38:69-119, d = .65 across 94 independent tests. 'Markedly increases' is a fair reading of a medium-to-large effect, not an overstatement.
Context-dependence of habit is solid, the simplification does not mislead, and the explanation names the mechanism (time, place, preceding event) instead of restating the option.
Editorial and correctly labelled. Safe, non-punitive, and 'do double to make up' is a real belief so the distractor earns its place.
Reasonable as simplified; option 2 is partly defensible but option 3 is clearly the better answer to the question as asked.

The question cannot be got wrong. 'How many days you turned up' is the definition of a streak, and the other three options are ruled out by simply knowing what the word means — no knowledge is tested. The point being made (a streak is not a fitness measure) is worth making, but make it the thing the reader has to work out: e.g. ask what a long streak does NOT tell you, or contrast two users with the same streak and different training.
Option 3 (people misjudge duration) is a real rival explanation rather than filler, which makes this a genuine question. Simplification is honest.

The claim is stated more firmly than the evidence supports, and probably backwards. Measured overnight muscle protein synthesis rates are LOW — lower than daytime and lower than post-absorptive morning values unless protein is given before sleep (Res et al. 2012; Trommelen & van Loon). Post-exercise synthesis is elevated across 24-48h, not concentrated in the hours you are asleep. 'Largely while you are asleep' is a gym truism, not a finding. What IS supportable: sleep restriction impairs training adaptation and growth-hormone pulses occur in slow-wave sleep. Rewrite around 'recovery depends on sleep' rather than 'most repair happens during sleep', or reject the item.

Standard adaptation framing, true at the level given. Option 0 is also true but less fundamental, which is the right shape for a distractor. Explanation adds the signal/response idea rather than restating.

Two problems. (1) Guessable: three of the four options are absolutes ('reliably', 'for anybody', 'always'), so the hedged one is identifiable as correct without knowing anything about sleep. Rewrite the distractors as specific, non-absolute claims. (2) The confidence label is wrong. `contested` requires the text to say the field disagrees; this explanation describes individual variation instead. And the field is not especially divided — Stutz et al. 2019 (Sports Med) found evening exercise does not generally harm sleep, with impairment mainly after vigorous exercise ending under an hour before bed. Relabel as `simplified` and consider naming that one-hour window, which is the actually useful fact here.
Definition is accurate, all four options are things the term could plausibly mean, and the explanation gives a usable test ('not enough to need recovering from').

Correctly kills the lactic-acid myth, which is worth the reader's attention. 'Follows the repair, not the effort' is a fair simplification of the damage-and-inflammation account, and option 3 is a genuinely tempting distractor.
True, useful, and safely framed — it defuses the 'no pain no gain' belief without shaming anyone. The two 'Yes' options are beliefs people really hold.

Source is Van Dongen et al. 2003, Sleep 26(2):117-26, and it does support the specific claim that subjective alertness ratings fail to track the objective deficit. The 0-vs-3 distinction is a real one, so the item tests something.
Sensible as simplified, no sleep-hygiene overclaiming, and the explanation gives the reason (you can decide to get up, not to fall asleep) rather than restating the option.
